meta.name: Red Hat Certified System Administrator (RHCSA)
meta.notes: [rhcsa batch 1: 18 scenario rewrites] [rhcsa batch 2: 21 scenario rewrites] [rhcsa batch 3 (final): 21 scenario rewrites] [rhcsa keyword-balance batch 1 (2026-05-23): 9 questions — distractor expansion adding shared stem keywords: rhcsa-010/012/013/020/023/025/032/045/052/053]

questions.question: A sysadmin sets file permissions for an audit-logged shell script: OWNER must have full read+write+execute, GROUP must have read+execute (no write), OTHER must have read only (no execute, no write). The mode is written as a 3-digit octal. Which command sets the permissions correctly?
options: `chmod 755 file` — sets `rwxr-xr-x` (group + other can execute); doesn't match (other should NOT execute)
`chmod 777 file` — sets `rwxrwxrwx` (everyone can write); too permissive
`chmod 644 file` — sets `rw-r--r--` (no exec for owner); too restrictive
`chmod 754 file` — owner 7 (rwx) + group 5 (r-x) + other 4 (r--) → exactly the rwxr-xr-- target
questions.explanation: Octal permissions: owner(rwx=7), group(r-x=5), others(r--=4) = 754. chmod 754 file sets this. Alternatively: chmod u=rwx,g=rx,o=r file. Use ls -l to verify.

questions.question: A custom systemd unit `myapp.service` is installed in `/etc/systemd/system/`. It's started manually with `systemctl start myapp` and works fine, BUT after reboot it doesn't start. The admin wants it to start automatically at boot. Which command creates the symlink in the WantedBy target so it starts at boot?
options: `systemctl activate myapp.service` — invalid; `activate` is not a systemctl verb
`systemctl enable myapp.service`
`systemctl start myapp.service` — starts ONCE for the current session; doesn't persist across reboots
`service myapp enable` — SysVinit-style, not systemd-native; on RHEL systemd is the init
questions.explanation: systemctl enable service: creates symlinks in /etc/systemd/system/multi-user.target.wants/ so service starts at boot. systemctl enable --now service: enable AND start immediately. systemctl disable: remove autostart. systemctl is-enabled: check status.

questions.question: A volume group `vg0` has 50 GB of free extents. The admin needs to create a LOGICAL VOLUME of 5 GB named `data` from `vg0`. Which command is the canonical syntax?
options: `lvcreate -L 5G -n data vg0`
`lvmkdir -s 5G vg0/data` — not a real lvm command
`mkvolume -L 5G -n data vg0` — not a real lvm command
`lvcreate -s 5G data vg0` — `-s` is for snapshots, and arguments are out of order
questions.explanation: lvcreate -L 5G -n data vg0: -L size, -n name, vg0 is the volume group. After: mkfs.xfs /dev/vg0/data then mount. -l for LE units: -l 100%FREE uses all free space. lvs: list logical volumes.

questions.question: An XFS filesystem on `/dev/vg0/data` is currently mounted on `/mnt/data` via the command line. To survive a reboot, the mount must be PERSISTENT. Which configuration file should the admin edit, and what line?
options: Append to `/etc/fstab`: `/dev/vg0/data /mnt/data xfs defaults 0 0`
`mountd --persistent` — not a real command
Append `mount …` to `/etc/rc.local` — discouraged on RHEL 7+; fstab is the canonical method
Run `mount /dev/vg0/data /mnt/data` — does NOT persist across reboots
questions.explanation: /etc/fstab format: device mountpoint filesystem options dump pass. defaults = rw,suid,dev,exec,auto,nouser,async. 0 0 = no dump, no fsck. After editing: mount -a to test without reboot. Use blkid to get UUID for more reliable mounting.

questions.question: RHEL ships SELinux enabled by default. SELinux enforces MANDATORY ACCESS CONTROL (MAC) on top of DAC — every process + file has a label (`type:role:user`) and policy decides which transitions are allowed. SELinux has THREE modes set via `/etc/selinux/config` or `setenforce`. Which describes SELinux and its modes?
options: A firewall — false; SELinux is a MAC layer, not a packet filter
Mandatory access control with three modes
Kernel module manager — false; that's lsmod / modprobe
An authentication system — false; SELinux is authorization, not authentication
questions.explanation: SELinux: mandatory access control beyond DAC (discretionary). Enforcing: production mode, violations blocked. Permissive: troubleshooting, logs denials but doesn't block. Disabled: requires reboot to change. /etc/selinux/config for persistent change. semanage, restorecon, ausearch -m avc: key tools. Enforcing, Permissive, Disabled

questions.question: A sysadmin needs to find EVERY file under `/var` owned by user `alice` (not group, but owner uid mapping to alice). Which command is correct?
options: `find /var -user alice` — searches recursively under /var for files whose owner is the user `alice`
`grep -r alice /var` — searches file CONTENTS for the literal string 'alice', not ownership
`ls -la /var | grep alice` — only the top-level directory of /var, doesn't recurse, and matches any literal text including filename
`locate -user alice /var` — locate doesn't have a `-user` flag
questions.explanation: find /var -user alice: finds all files owned by alice. find /var -group devs: by group. find /var -perm /4000: find SUID files. find /var -mtime -7: modified in last 7 days. find /var -size +100M: files > 100MB. -exec rm {} \; to act on results.

questions.question: A RHEL host runs `firewalld`. The admin needs to LIST the active firewall config: enabled zones, allowed services/ports, sources, masquerade settings — all in one human-readable view. Which `firewall-cmd` invocation produces this?
options: `iptables -L` — shows iptables rules; firewalld has its own data model on top
`netstat -tuln` — shows LISTENING sockets, not firewall config
`firewall-cmd --list-all`
`ss -tulnp` — shows sockets + processes, not firewall rules
questions.explanation: firewall-cmd --list-all: shows active zone, interfaces, sources, services, ports. --list-ports: ports only. --list-services: services only. Add port: firewall-cmd --add-port=8080/tcp --permanent then --reload. firewall-cmd --zone=public --add-service=http --permanent.

questions.question: An XFS filesystem mounted at `/mnt/data` lives on an LV that was just extended by 10 GiB (`lvextend -L +10G vg0/data`). The filesystem itself still reports the old size. Which command grows the XFS to fill the LV?
options: `xfs_growfs /mnt/data`
`xfs_expand /mnt/data` — not a real command
`resize2fs /mnt/data` — wrong filesystem; resize2fs is for ext2/3/4
`fsck -r /mnt/data` — filesystem check, doesn't resize
questions.explanation: Expand LV: lvextend -L +10G /dev/vg0/data. Extend XFS: xfs_growfs /mnt/data (use mount point, not device). XFS can be grown while mounted. ext4: resize2fs /dev/vg0/data (use device). Always expand LV first, then filesystem.

questions.question: A sysadmin wants a `nightly-backup.sh` to run every night at 02:30. The user-level scheduling subsystem in RHEL is `cron`. Which describes the purpose AND the canonical command to edit the current user's crontab?
options: Backup-only scheduler — false; cron schedules any command
Schedule recurring tasks (minute / hour / day-of-month / month /
Init-system replacement — false; cron is a scheduler, not an init
Network-only scheduler — false; cron is general-purpose
questions.explanation: crontab format: */5 * * * * /path/to/script (every 5 min). Fields: min(0-59) hour(0-23) day(1-31) month(1-12) weekday(0-7). crontab -l: list. crontab -r: remove. /etc/crontab: system cron with user field. /etc/cron.d/: additional cron files. systemd timers: modern alternative. crontab -e, format: min hour day month weekday cmd

questions.question: Create a new user `bob` with UID 1500, default shell `/bin/bash`, and a home directory `/home/bob`. The home directory should be created automatically with the user. Which `useradd` invocation is correct?
options: `useradd bob --uid 1500 --home /home/bob` — creates the user but `--uid` and `--home` are not valid short flags; correct flags are `-u` and `-d`; also omits `-s` for shell
`useradd -u 1500 -m -s /bin/bash bob` — specifies UID 1500 (`-u`), creates the home directory (`-m`), sets the default shell (`-s`), and then the username; canonical invocation
`adduser -uid 1500 -shell /bin/bash bob` — `adduser` is a higher-level interactive wrapper; `-uid` is not a valid flag; use `useradd` for scriptable user creation with explicit UID
`usermod -u 1500 -s /bin/bash bob` — `usermod` modifies an existing user record; `bob` must already exist; `useradd` creates the user and home directory from scratch
questions.explanation: useradd -u 1500 -m -s /bin/bash bob: -u UID, -m create home, -s shell. Set password: passwd bob. -g primary group: -g groupname. -G supplementary groups: -G wheel,docker. View: id bob. Modify existing user: usermod. Delete: userdel -r bob (remove home).

questions.question: A shared `/tmp` directory has world-writable permissions (1777). Without an extra flag, any user could delete any other user's files in `/tmp`. The 'sticky bit' on a directory restricts this so ONLY the file's owner (or root) can delete it. Which describes the sticky bit's effect?
options: Only the owner (or root) can DELETE files in that directory
Prevents anyone from writing — false; that's a permission, not the sticky bit
Sets SGID on new files — that's the SGID bit, not sticky
Makes contents immutable — false; that's `chattr +i`
questions.explanation: Sticky bit (chmod +t or mode 1xxx): files in directory can only be deleted by: file owner, directory owner, or root. Common on /tmp (world-writable but users can't delete each other's files). ls -ld shows 't' in others execute position. chmod 1777 /shared sets sticky+rwxrwxrwx.

questions.question: Set a STATIC IP `192.168.1.10/24` with gateway `192.168.1.1` and DNS `8.8.8.8` on interface `eth0` using NetworkManager. The change must persist across reboots. Which commands?
options: `nmcli con mod eth0 ipv4.addresses 192.168.1.10/24 ipv4.gateway 192.168.1.1 ipv4.dns 8.8.8.8 ipv4.method manual && nmcli con up eth0` — persistent NetworkManager configuration

`ip addr add 192.168.1.10/24 dev eth0 && ip route add default via 192.168.1.1` — sets the address and gateway temporarily, but DNS (8.8.8.8) requires a separate `/etc/resolv.conf` edit; lost on reboot
`ifconfig eth0 192.168.1.10 netmask 255.255.255.0 gateway 192.168.1.1` — `ifconfig` is deprecated and `gateway` is not a valid `ifconfig` argument; DNS 8.8.8.8 would still need manual configuration
`vi /etc/network/interfaces` — the Debian/Ubuntu approach to setting IP, gateway, and DNS persistently; RHEL uses NetworkManager with `nmcli` or `nmtui`, not `/etc/network/interfaces`
questions.explanation: nmcli con mod CONNECTION ipv4.addresses IP/MASK ipv4.gateway GW ipv4.dns DNS ipv4.method manual. Then nmcli con up CONNECTION. Persistent. nmcli con show: list connections. nmcli device status: device states. Alternatively: edit /etc/NetworkManager/system-connections/CONNECTION.nmconnection.

questions.question: A systemd-running RHEL host. The admin wants LIVE tailing of ALL systemd journal entries (kernel + services + user) as they happen — so they can watch a service starting in another terminal. Which command?
options: `tail -f /var/log/messages` — tails the legacy rsyslog file in live mode but misses systemd-journald entries from user services; incomplete coverage of all systemd units
`journalctl -f` — follow mode; live tailing of ALL systemd-journald entries: kernel messages, system services, and user-session units
`dmesg --follow` — live tailing of the kernel ring buffer only; does not include systemd user service or application journal entries
`cat /var/log/syslog` — reads the Debian/Ubuntu syslog file; does not exist on RHEL; does not provide live tailing of systemd journal entries
questions.explanation: journalctl -f: follow (like tail -f). journalctl -u nginx: logs for specific unit. journalctl -xe: recent logs with explanations. journalctl --since '1 hour ago': time filter. journalctl -p err: error level and above. journalctl --disk-usage: storage used. /var/log/messages: traditional syslog, may still exist.

questions.question: Schedule a ONE-OFF (not recurring) task to run a backup script at 15:00 today. After running, it should NOT re-run. Which utility is correct?
options: `systemd-run --on-calendar='15:00' …` — runs once but creates a transient unit; works but isn't the classical RHCSA answer
`crontab -e` + `0 15 * * *` — that's RECURRING every day at 15:00, not one-off
`once --time=15:00 …` — not a real command
`at 15:00` then enter the command and press Ctrl+D — the canonical one-off scheduler (`at` daemon)
questions.explanation: at command: at 15:00 (enter commands, Ctrl+D to finish). at now + 1 hour. atq: list scheduled at jobs. atrm JOB_NUM: remove. Service: atd must be running. For recurring: use cron. at is for one-time delayed execution.

questions.question: The `/etc/sudoers` file defines which users can run which commands as root. Editing it directly with `vi` is DANGEROUS — a syntax error locks out sudo. A wrapper tool opens the file in an editor, validates syntax on save, and rejects bad edits. Which tool, and what's `/etc/sudoers` for?
options: Firewall — wrong file
PAM auth — different file
SSH authorized_keys — different file
`/etc/sudoers` defines sudo
questions.explanation: visudo: opens /etc/sudoers in editor with syntax checking — prevents saving invalid syntax that would break sudo for all users. %wheel ALL=(ALL) ALL: all wheel group members can sudo. User bob can restart nginx without password: bob ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD: /bin/systemctl restart nginx. /etc/sudoers.d/: drop-in files.

questions.question: An SELinux policy admin wants to LIST every SELinux boolean related to `httpd` (e.g., `httpd_can_network_connect`, `httpd_enable_homedirs`). The output must include current ON/OFF state. Which command?
options: `selinux list httpd` — not a real subcommand
`getsebool -a | grep httpd`
`sestatus --booleans httpd` — not a sestatus flag
`ls /etc/selinux/booleans/httpd` — wrong path / wrong layout
questions.explanation: getsebool -a: list all booleans with current values. getsebool httpd_can_network_connect: specific boolean. setsebool -P httpd_can_network_connect on: set persistently (-P). Common booleans: httpd_can_network_connect (allow Apache to make outbound connections), httpd_use_nfs (allow serving NFS-mounted content).

questions.question: An admin needs to add user `alice` to the existing supplementary group `wheel` (so she gains sudo privileges) WITHOUT removing her from any other groups. Which command preserves existing group memberships and adds wheel?
options: `groupadd wheel alice` — `groupadd` creates groups, doesn't add users
`addgroup alice wheel` — Debian/Ubuntu syntax, not RHEL
`usermod -aG wheel alice`
`gpasswd -a wheel alice` — argument order reversed; correct order is `gpasswd -a alice wheel`
questions.explanation: usermod -aG wheel username: -a (append, don't replace other groups), -G (supplementary group). Without -a: replaces ALL supplementary groups! gpasswd -a username wheel: alternative. id username: verify. User needs to re-login for group change to take effect (or: newgrp wheel in current session).

questions.question: An admin partitions a spare disk as `/dev/sdb2` and wants to add it as additional swap space — both ACTIVATED NOW and PERSISTED across reboots. Which sequence?
options: `swapformat /dev/sdb2 && swapon` — not a real command
`fdisk /dev/sdb2 --swap` — fdisk doesn't have `--swap`
`mkswap /dev/sdb2` (format as swap), `swapon /dev/sdb2`
`mkswap` then `systemctl restart swapd` — `swapd` is not a service
questions.explanation: Steps: (1) fdisk/parted to create partition with type 82 (Linux swap). (2) mkswap /dev/sdb2. (3) swapon /dev/sdb2 (immediate). (4) /etc/fstab: '/dev/sdb2 swap swap defaults 0 0'. swapon -s: show active swap. free -h: memory + swap stats. swapfile: dd + mkswap + swapon works too. add to /etc/fstab

questions.question: Linux name-to-IP resolution consults a CONFIGURABLE list of sources (by default `files` then `dns`, defined in `/etc/nsswitch.conf`). The `files` source reads from `/etc/hosts`. An entry in `/etc/hosts` like `10.0.5.42 internal.example.com` overrides DNS for that name. What is `/etc/hosts`?
options: Replaces /etc/resolv.conf — false; resolv.conf configures DNS servers, hosts maps names locally
Localhost-only — false; can store any local override
Hostname-only — false; that's `/etc/hostname`
Local hostname → IP override map
questions.explanation: /etc/hosts: IP FQDN aliases per line. /etc/nsswitch.conf hosts: files dns — 'files' means check /etc/hosts first. For testing: add temporary entry. /etc/resolv.conf: DNS server configuration (nameserver IP, domain, search). hostnamectl: set system hostname. dnsdomainname: show domain. checked before DNS per /etc/nsswitch.conf

questions.question: A RHEL server should boot DIRECTLY into the multi-user (non-graphical) target — equivalent to the old SysVinit runlevel 3 — without a GUI. The change must persist across reboots. Which systemd command?
options: `init 3` — switches the current runlevel to multi-user immediately but does not persist the target across reboots; the default target remains unchanged
`systemctl set-default multi-user.target` — sets the persistent default target so the host boots into multi-user (non-graphical) on every subsequent reboot
`runlevel set 3` — `runlevel` only reports the current and previous runlevel targets; it has no `set` subcommand for changing the default
`systemctl default --target=multi-user` — incorrect invocation; `systemctl default` switches to the current default target immediately without accepting a `--target` argument for persistent change
questions.explanation: systemctl set-default multi-user.target: non-graphical multi-user (like runlevel 3). graphical.target: desktop (runlevel 5). rescue.target: single-user maintenance. systemctl isolate multi-user.target: switch immediately (kills graphical). systemctl get-default: check current default target.

questions.question: An admin archives `/etc/myapp/` into a single compressed file `archive.tar.gz` and verifies what's in it. Which command CREATES the gzipped tar archive?
options: `tar -czvf archive.tar.gz /etc/myapp/`
`tar -xzvf archive.tar.gz` — `x` is EXTRACT, not create
`gzip -r ... > archive.tar.gz` — gzip alone doesn't produce a tar; produces individual .gz files
`zip -r archive.tar.gz ...` — uses ZIP format, not tar.gz; misleading filename
questions.explanation: tar -czvf: -c create, -z gzip compression, -v verbose, -f filename. Extract: tar -xzvf archive.tar.gz. List contents: tar -tzvf. To specific dir: tar -xzvf archive.tar.gz -C /target/. .tar.bz2: use -j instead of -z. .tar.xz: use -J. --exclude=PATTERN to exclude files.

questions.question: A new RHEL host needs to access Red Hat repos for `dnf update`. Without a subscription, only the local install ISO repos are available. The customer's Red Hat account has a subscription pool. Which describes a RHEL subscription and the registration command?
options: Network-only license — false
Firewall license — false
Entitlement granting access to Red Hat repos +
License file in `/etc/redhat-release` — false; that file is just OS version info
questions.explanation: RHEL subscription: required for yum/dnf updates and support. subscription-manager register: authenticate with RHSM (Red Hat Subscription Management) or Satellite. subscription-manager status: check. subscription-manager repos --list: see available repos. In RHEL 8+: insights-client --register for Red Hat Insights. register with subscription-manager register

questions.question: A web server's DocumentRoot was moved from `/var/www/html` to `/srv/web`. Apache refuses to read it because the new path has the wrong SELinux file context. The admin wants to APPLY the correct default contexts for `/srv/web` based on the SELinux policy database. Which command?
options: `restorecon -Rv /srv/web` — recursively re-applies the default SELinux file contexts from the policy database to `/srv/web`, correcting the context mismatch without changing the policy
`selinux --restore /srv/web` — not a valid command; the correct tool for restoring default SELinux contexts from the policy database is `restorecon`, not `selinux`
`chcon --default /srv/web` — `chcon` can apply an explicit context but `--default` is not a standard flag; `chcon` changes are also not persistent across `restorecon` runs from the policy database
`sestatus --restore` — `sestatus` displays the current SELinux status and mode; it has no `--restore` flag and cannot reapply default contexts from the policy database
questions.explanation: restorecon -Rv /path: -R recursive, -v verbose. Restores contexts based on policy defaults (/etc/selinux/targeted/contexts/files/). Use after: moving files (context doesn't follow move), creating new files in wrong location. matchpathcon -V: verify contexts. semanage fcontext: add custom file context rules.

questions.question: Two ways to create 'a link' on Linux. Hard link: SECOND directory entry pointing at the SAME inode (same data); requires same filesystem; can't link directories. Symbolic link: SEPARATE file whose content is a TEXTUAL path to the target; can cross filesystems and link directories. Which describes the difference?
options: Symlinks share inode — false; hard links share inode
Hard links share the inode (same data),
Hard links cross filesystems — false; opposite
No difference — false
questions.explanation: Hard link: ln source dest. Same inode. Deleting original doesn't break link. Cannot link directories (normally). Same filesystem only. Soft link: ln -s /path/to/source dest. Different inode (stores path). Breaks if source deleted/moved. Can cross filesystems, link directories, point to non-existent paths. symlinks store a path and can cross filesystems

questions.question: RHEL 8+ uses `chrony` (not `ntpd`) as the default time-sync daemon. The admin wants to ADD an upstream NTP server `time.nist.gov` to chrony's config and reload. Which approach?
options: `systemctl start ntpd` — starts the legacy `ntpd` daemon; RHEL 8+ uses `chronyd` by default; `ntpd` cannot add `time.nist.gov` as a server source when `chronyd` owns the socket
`ntpdate -u time.nist.gov` — a one-shot legacy time adjustment; does not add `time.nist.gov` as a persistent server to `chrony`'s source pool
`timedatectl set-ntp true` — enables NTP synchronisation using the default server pool; does not add a specific server like `time.nist.gov iburst` to chrony's configuration
Add `server time.nist.gov iburst` to `/etc/chrony.conf`, then restart `chronyd` with `systemctl restart chronyd` — the canonical way to add an upstream time server to chrony
questions.explanation: chrony (RHEL 7+): /etc/chrony.conf — server ntp.example.com iburst. systemctl restart chronyd. chronyc sources: show NTP sources. chronyc tracking: show sync status. timedatectl: set timezone and check sync status. timedatectl list-timezones. timedatectl set-timezone America/New_York. chronyd preferred over ntpd in RHEL 7+.

questions.question: Standard UNIX file permissions allow ONE owner + ONE group + other. A team of 5 users needs DIFFERENT permissions per user on the same file — beyond the rwx/owner/group/other model. A POSIX feature lets you set per-user / per-group permissions on a file via `setfacl`. Which feature?
options: SELinux policy — different layer (MAC, not granular DAC)
firewalld zone — wrong category
iptables rule — wrong category
POSIX Access Control Lists (ACLs)
questions.explanation: ACL: setfacl -m u:USER:PERMS file, setfacl -m g:GROUP:PERMS file, setfacl -m o::PERMS file. -x: remove entry. -b: remove all ACLs. -R: recursive. Default ACL for directory (-d): inherited by new files. getfacl file: shows all ACL entries. Filesystem needs acl mount option (default on ext4/xfs in RHEL). setfacl -m u:alice:rw file grants per-user access

questions.question: A router shows `10.2.0.0/24 via 192.168.1.254` is not reachable. The admin needs to add a route for that network. They want both: TEMPORARY (current session, lost on reboot) and PERSISTENT (survives reboot). Which approach?
options: `netstat route add` — `netstat` doesn't add routes
`route add NETWORK/MASK GW` — `route` is deprecated on modern RHEL; doesn't persist
Temporary: `ip route add 10.2.0.0/24 via 192.168.1.254`
`ifconfig route add` — ifconfig doesn't manage routes
questions.explanation: Temporary: ip route add 192.168.10.0/24 via 10.0.0.1 (lost on reboot). Permanent (NetworkManager): nmcli con mod CONNECTION ipv4.routes '192.168.10.0/24 10.0.0.1' then nmcli con up CONNECTION. Or edit connection file. ip route show: display routing table. Permanent: nmcli con mod CON ipv4.routes

questions.question: A user creates a new file with `touch /tmp/test`. The default permissions are NOT 0666 (rw-rw-rw-) — they're filtered by a shell setting that defines which bits are SUBTRACTED. With umask 022, new files default to 0644 (rw-r--r--), new directories to 0755. What is `umask`?
options: Which users can execute — wrong concept
SELinux context — different mechanism
Minimum password length — different setting
Default permission bits SUBTRACTED from 0666
questions.explanation: umask: subtracted from max (files=666, dirs=777). umask 022: files=644, dirs=755 (common default). umask 027: files=640, dirs=750 (more secure). Set in: /etc/profile (system), ~/.bashrc (user). umask without args: shows current. Doesn't affect existing files.

questions.question: An admin needs to find the `httpd` package and install it on RHEL 8/9 (which uses `dnf` as package manager — `yum` is now a compat-symlink). Which command pair?
options: `yum search httpd; yum install httpd` — works (yum is a compatibility wrapper to dnf on RHEL 8/9), but `dnf` is the canonical answer
`rpm -search httpd` — `rpm` doesn't search remote repos
`apt search httpd` — Debian/Ubuntu tool, not RHEL
`dnf search httpd` then `dnf install httpd` — the canonical RHEL 8/9 invocation
questions.explanation: dnf search httpd: find packages. dnf info httpd: details. dnf install httpd: install. dnf remove httpd: uninstall. dnf update: update all. dnf upgrade: update + obsoletes. dnf list installed: installed packages. dnf provides /usr/sbin/httpd: which package provides file. dnf history: transaction history.

questions.question: A disk-space investigator wants to know HOW MUCH disk space the `/var/log` directory is consuming. `df` shows free space per FILESYSTEM, which doesn't directly answer the per-DIRECTORY question. Which command answers per-directory?
options: `df -h /var/log` — filesystem-level usage; says nothing per directory
`du -sh /var/log`
`fdisk -l` — partition layout, no usage
`ls -lh /var/log` — lists files (not recursive size of subdirectories)
questions.explanation: du -sh /path: -s summary (total), -h human readable. du -h --max-depth=1 /var: one level deep. du -sh *: all items in current dir. df -h: filesystem disk space (mounted filesystems). df -i: inode usage. lsblk: block devices. fdisk -l: partition table.

questions.question: An admin needs to enforce a PASSWORD-AGING policy on user `alice`: max age 90 days, warn 7 days before expiry. The command modifies `/etc/shadow` aging fields. Which?
options: `passwd --expire alice` — IMMEDIATELY expires, doesn't set max age policy
`chage -M 90 -W 7 alice`
`usermod --password-age` — `usermod` doesn't have password-aging flags; that's chage's job
`passwdage --set` — not a real command
questions.explanation: chage -M 90: max days before password must change. -m 1: minimum days between changes. -W 7: warn 7 days before expiry. -l username: list current aging info. -E 2025-12-31: account expiry date. -I 30: days after expiry before account locked. /etc/login.defs: PASS_MAX_DAYS for system default.

questions.question: A sysadmin reads `/proc/cpuinfo`, `/proc/meminfo`, `/proc/<pid>/status`, `/proc/sys/...`. None of these files exist on disk — they're generated ON DEMAND by the kernel exposing live state via a virtual filesystem. Which describes `/proc`?
options: The `/proc` directory is a core-dump area for kernel crash files — false; core dumps go to `/var/lib/systemd/coredump` or a `core_pattern` path; `/proc` holds live kernel state files
The `/proc` directory is persistent storage for system logs — false; `/proc` is not persistent; it is a virtual filesystem in RAM exposing live kernel and process state
The `/proc` directory is the startup-script directory for legacy init — false; startup scripts live in `/etc/init.d`; `/proc` is a virtual filesystem exposing live kernel and process files
The `/proc` filesystem is a virtual / synthetic filesystem created by the kernel at boot that exposes live kernel state, process info, and hardware details as readable pseudo-files
questions.explanation: /proc: read kernel state. /proc/sys/net/ipv4/ip_forward: IP forwarding. sysctl -w net.ipv4.ip_forward=1: change via sysctl. /etc/sysctl.conf: persistent changes. /proc/PID/: process memory maps, open files, status. cat /proc/cpuinfo: CPU details. /proc/mounts: current mounts.

questions.question: Schedule `backup.sh` to run every WEEKDAY (Mon-Fri) at 08:00. Cron's 5-field schedule is `minute hour day-of-month month day-of-week`. Day-of-week 1-5 = Mon-Fri. Which crontab entry?
options: `systemd-timer --daily --weekdays 8am` — not a real syntax
`0 8 * * 1-5 /path/to/script`
`schedule --daily ...` — not a real command
`8:00 weekdays …` — not the crontab syntax
questions.explanation: Cron format: MIN HOUR DOM MON DOW COMMAND. 0 8 * * 1-5 = minute 0, hour 8, any day, any month, Mon-Fri (1-5). crontab -e: edit user crontab. Redirect output: 0 8 * * 1-5 /script >> /var/log/script.log 2>&1. Run as root: use /etc/crontab with user field.

questions.question: An admin needs to see (a) every TCP/UDP socket in LISTEN state, (b) the local + remote address + port, (c) the process / pid / executable that owns each socket. Which command provides all of this in ONE invocation?
options: `netstat -r` — routing table only, no sockets/processes
`ss -tulnp`
`ip link show` — interface state, no sockets
`ifconfig -a` — interface config, no sockets
questions.explanation: ss -tulnp: -t TCP, -u UDP, -l listening, -n numeric (no name resolution), -p show process. Shows: port, state, PID, process name. Requires root for all PIDs. netstat -tulnp: older equivalent (net-tools package). lsof -i :80: what's using port 80. firewall-cmd --list-ports: what's open in firewall.

questions.question: An admin sets a tunable `net.ipv4.ip_forward=1` temporarily via `sysctl -w net.ipv4.ip_forward=1` or `echo 1 > /proc/sys/net/ipv4/ip_forward`. Both are LOST on reboot. To make the change persistent: which file + reload?
options: `sysctl --permanent` — not a real flag
`echo … > /proc/sys/…` — runtime only, lost on reboot
`modprobe --persist` — `modprobe` loads modules, not sysctl values
Add `net.ipv4.ip_forward=1` to `/etc/sysctl.conf` (or `
questions.explanation: Temporary: sysctl -w net.ipv4.ip_forward=1 (or echo 1 > /proc/sys/net/ipv4/ip_forward). Persistent: add 'net.ipv4.ip_forward = 1' to /etc/sysctl.conf or create /etc/sysctl.d/99-custom.conf. Apply without reboot: sysctl -p (reads /etc/sysctl.conf) or sysctl --system (reads all sysctl.d files).

questions.question: Two common `ps` flag conventions exist on Linux. `ps aux` (BSD-style, no leading hyphen) shows all processes including TTY, CPU %, MEM %, START, TIME, COMMAND. `ps -ef` (SysV-style, leading hyphen) shows UID, PID, PPID, STIME, TTY, TIME, CMD. Which describes the difference?
options: `ps aux`
`ps aux` BSD-only — false; works on Linux too
`ps -ef` shows only root processes — false; shows all unless filtered
Identical output — false; different column sets and origins (BSD vs SysV)
questions.explanation: ps aux: a=all users, u=user format, x=no terminal. Shows CPU%, MEM%, virtual/resident size. ps -ef: e=all processes, f=full format. Shows PPID (parent PID). Both useful: aux for resource usage, -ef for parent-child relationships. ps auxf: combined with process tree. ps -ef uses UNIX syntax showing PPID

questions.question: An admin wants to set `PROJECT_HOME=/srv/proj` for ALL users system-wide. The setting must be PERSISTENT (survive reboot) and available to logins via any shell (bash, zsh, sh). Which file should they edit?
options: `systemctl set-env` — only for systemd's environment, not user shells
`env --system` — not a real subcommand
`~/.bashrc` — per-user, bash-only, not system-wide
Add `export PROJECT_HOME=/srv/proj` to `/etc/environment`
questions.explanation: /etc/environment: simple KEY=VALUE format (no bash syntax), loaded for all users. /etc/profile.d/*.sh: shell scripts sourced for all login shells (can use export, functions). ~/.bashrc: user-specific, non-login shells. ~/.bash_profile: user-specific, login shells. systemd services: set in service unit [Service] Environment=.

questions.question: An admin wants to run a BATCH JOB at LOWER CPU scheduling priority so it doesn't slow down interactive users. Standard niceness scale: -20 (highest priority) to +19 (lowest). The default is 0. A wrapper command launches a process with adjusted niceness. Which command?
options: Network reachability test — that's `ping`
`nice -n 10 long-running-job.sh`
SIGTERM — that's `kill -TERM`
Friendly-message display — wrong command
questions.explanation: Niceness: -20 (highest priority) to 19 (lowest). nice -n 5 ./heavy_job: run with niceness +5. nice -n -5 ./critical: higher priority (root only). renice 5 PID: change running process. Useful for: background batch jobs (high nice), critical services (low nice). Affects CPU scheduler only, not I/O.

questions.question: A RHEL host needs to mount an NFS share `nfsserver:/share` at `/mnt/nfs`. The mount must be PERSISTENT (survives reboot). Which sequence?
options: `mount -t nfs nfsserver:/share /mnt/nfs`
`mount --type=nfs nfsserver/share /mnt` — wrong syntax (missing colon)
`smbmount` — SMB, not NFS
`nfsmount` — not a real command
questions.explanation: Temporary: mount -t nfs nfsserver:/share /mnt/nfs. Persistent /etc/fstab: nfsserver:/share /mnt/nfs nfs defaults,_netdev 0 0. _netdev: wait for network before mounting. nfsstat: show NFS stats. showmount -e nfsserver: list server exports. Install nfs-utils first: dnf install nfs-utils. add to /etc/fstab for persistence

questions.question: An admin needs to kill every running instance of a misbehaving process called `myapp` (could be multiple PIDs). The lookup is by process NAME, not PID. Two interchangeable commands do this. Which?
options: `terminate myapp` — not a real command
`kill -name myapp` — `kill` only takes PIDs, no name flag
`stop myapp` — not a real command
`killall myapp` OR `pkill myapp`
questions.explanation: killall httpd: send SIGTERM to all processes named httpd. pkill -f 'python script.py': match by full command line. kill PID: by process ID. kill -9 PID: SIGKILL (force, cannot be caught). kill -l: list signals. pkill -u username: kill all processes by user. SIGTERM (15): graceful. SIGKILL (9): force.

questions.question: A volume `/dev/sdb1` failed to mount cleanly after an unexpected shutdown. The admin needs to repair the filesystem. fsck MUST run on an UNMOUNTED filesystem (running it on mounted = corruption risk). The `-y` flag answers yes to all prompts. Which command?
options: `mkfs --check` — `mkfs` CREATES filesystems, doesn't repair
`fsck` while mounted — DANGEROUS; can corrupt the filesystem
Unmount first, then `fsck -y /dev/sdb1`
`tune2fs --repair` — `tune2fs` tunes parameters, doesn't repair
questions.explanation: CRITICAL: fsck only on unmounted filesystems. -y: auto-answer yes to all repair prompts. For root filesystem: run from rescue mode or use e2fsck (ext4). xfs_repair /dev/sdb1: for XFS. fsck on mounted FS will corrupt data. Boot to rescue: systemctl rescue. e2fsck -p: auto-fix safe issues.

questions.question: Linux stores user accounts in TWO files: (A) world-readable, listing UID + GID + GECOS + home + shell — NO password. (B) ROOT-readable only, holding hashed password + aging fields. The split protects password hashes from world readers while keeping basic user info available. Which mapping?
options: `/etc/passwd` (world-readable
Identical files — false
/etc/shadow deprecated — false; still used
Both store plaintext — false; passwd has 'x' placeholder, shadow has hash
questions.explanation: /etc/passwd format: username:x:UID:GID:comment:home:shell. /etc/shadow: username:HASH:lastchange:min:max:warn:inactive:expire. HASH format: $6$ = SHA-512. chage: modify shadow aging. pwck: check passwd consistency. unshadow: combine for cracking (John the Ripper). /etc/shadow stores hashed passwords (root-only)

questions.question: An admin wants to log in to `server` via SSH WITHOUT a password — using a key pair. Generate the keypair on the client, copy the public key to the server's `~/.ssh/authorized_keys`. Which canonical commands?
options: `ssh-agent` — agent forwarding, not key generation
`sshd --add-key` — sshd is the server daemon, doesn't add keys this way
`ssh-keygen -t rsa -b 4096` (generate client keypair)
`ssh --generate-keys` — not a real flag
questions.explanation: Steps: (1) ssh-keygen -t ed25519 (modern) or -t rsa -b 4096. (2) ssh-copy-id user@server: copies ~/.ssh/id_*.pub to server's ~/.ssh/authorized_keys. (3) Test: ssh user@server (no password). Server: /etc/ssh/sshd_config PubkeyAuthentication yes (default). ~/.ssh permissions: 700 (dir), 600 (private key), 644 (pub key).

questions.question: A sysadmin needs the FULL METADATA of a file: inode number, byte size, block count, IO block size, owner UID + GID, mode (octal + symbolic), access / modify / change times, links count, device, type. Which command displays all of this?
options: System-wide CPU + memory stats — different tool (`vmstat`, `top`)
`stat <file>`
Network packet stats — different tool (`ifconfig -s`, `ip -s link`)
Per-CPU usage — different tool (`mpstat`)
questions.explanation: stat file: inode, size, device, permission (0644), links, UID, GID, atime (last access), mtime (last modification), ctime (last metadata change). stat -f /mnt: filesystem statistics. Use for: audit trails, inode investigation, checking when file was modified vs accessed. permissions, owner, and access/modify/change timestamps

questions.question: A RHEL host without internet access needs to install packages from a local DVD or NFS mount. The admin must configure a LOCAL repo so `dnf install` reads from `file:///path/to/repo`. Which steps?
options: Run `createrepo /path` only — generates the local repomd.xml metadata, but `dnf` still needs a `.repo` file in `/etc/yum.repos.d/` pointing to that local path to discover the repository
Use `localrepo --add /path` — not a real command; local repositories must be configured via `createrepo` for metadata plus a `/etc/yum.repos.d/local.repo` file
Copy the RPM files to `/var/cache/dnf` — these are `dnf`'s download cache directories; placing RPMs there does not register them as an installable local repository
Run `createrepo` to generate local `repomd.xml` metadata, then create `/etc/yum.repos.d/local.repo` pointing to the local path, and run `dnf install <package>`
questions.explanation: Create repo file: [local-repo] name=Local Repository baseurl=file:///mnt/iso/Packages enabled=1 gpgcheck=0. dnf clean all && dnf repolist. createrepo_c /path: create repo metadata from RPMs. Mount ISO: mount -o loop rhel.iso /mnt/iso. Useful for: air-gapped systems, offline patching.

questions.question: firewalld organises traffic policy into ZONES — each is a NAMED TRUST LEVEL (drop, block, public, external, internal, trusted, work, home, dmz). Network interfaces and source addresses are bound to a zone; the zone's services + ports + rich-rules apply to traffic matching that binding. The default zone on a fresh RHEL is `public`. Which describes zones?
options: Single global ruleset — false; multiple zones
Zones apply only to virtual interfaces — false; both physical + virtual
Named trust levels with their own rules
Default is `home` — false; default is `public`
questions.explanation: Zones: trusted→public→home→work→dmz→drop (descending trust). firewall-cmd --get-default-zone. firewall-cmd --set-default-zone=trusted. firewall-cmd --zone=dmz --add-service=http. firewall-cmd --get-active-zones: zones + assigned interfaces. Per-zone rules apply to assigned interface's traffic. default zone is 'public'

questions.question: A RHEL admin has forgotten the root password. The boot disk is intact. They need to reset it WITHOUT a USB rescue medium — using the GRUB menu. Which sequence resets the root password?
options: `systemctl set-password root` — not a real command
Boot from USB only — false; in-place recovery is possible
Interrupt GRUB at boot, edit the kernel line to APPEND `
`grub2-rescue --reset-password` — not a real command
questions.explanation: Reset root password: (1) GRUB screen → 'e' to edit. (2) Find linux line → append 'rd.break' (interrupts before root mount). (3) mount -o remount,rw /sysroot. (4) chroot /sysroot. (5) passwd root. (6) touch /.autorelabel (SELinux relabel). (7) exit twice → reboot. SELinux relabel required or login fails.

questions.question: Older RHEL ran boot-time scripts via `/etc/rc.local`. Modern RHEL is systemd-native. `/etc/rc.local` is now LEGACY — present for compat but disabled by default; the canonical approach is creating a systemd unit. What's the difference?
options: `/etc/rc.local`
rc.local preferred — false; opposite
systemd can't run shell scripts — false; ExecStart can run any executable
Identical — false; rc.local lacks dependency tracking + journald logging
questions.explanation: rc.local: /etc/rc.d/rc.local must be executable (chmod +x). Runs after all services. No error handling, no parallelism. Systemd service: create /etc/systemd/system/myscript.service [Service] ExecStart=/path/script [Install] WantedBy=multi-user.target. Enable: systemctl enable myscript. Better for production. systemd services offer dependency and recovery management

questions.question: An Apache (`httpd`) instance hosts MULTIPLE domain names from one server (`example.com`, `blog.example.com`, `shop.example.com`). Each domain has its own document root and config. The standard pattern is one `.conf` file per site under `/etc/httpd/conf.d/`. Which approach?
options: Edit `/etc/httpd/conf/httpd.conf` main block only — works but doesn't isolate per-site config
Only one site per Apache — false; that's the whole point of VirtualHost
Use nginx instead — Apache fully supports virtual hosting
Create `/etc/httpd/conf.d/mysite.conf` containing `<VirtualHost *:80> ServerName …
questions.explanation: VirtualHost: <VirtualHost *:80> ServerName www.example.com DocumentRoot /var/www/example ErrorLog /var/log/httpd/example-error.log </VirtualHost>. Each site: separate .conf in /etc/httpd/conf.d/. httpd -t: syntax check. systemctl reload httpd: apply. SELinux: chcon -Rt httpd_sys_content_t /var/www/example or use restorecon.

questions.question: A RHEL host's `/var/log/journal` has grown to 8 GB. The admin wants to KEEP recent journal data but cap total on-disk size at 500 MB — removing the oldest entries until under the cap. Which journalctl command?
options: `journalctl --vacuum-size=500M`
Increases max size — false; that's `SystemMaxUse=` in journald.conf
Backs up to backup folder — false; vacuum doesn't back up
Compresses with gzip — false; vacuum doesn't compress
questions.explanation: Journal management: journalctl --vacuum-size=500M (immediate cleanup). Persistent size limit: /etc/systemd/journald.conf → SystemMaxUse=500M → systemctl restart systemd-journald. journalctl --rotate: rotate log files. RuntimeMaxUse: volatile storage limit. Logs stored in /var/log/journal/ (persistent) or /run/log/journal/ (volatile).

questions.question: RHEL 8 introduced Stratis — a USER-SPACE storage management system on top of XFS + dm-thin. The admin wants to create a POOL from `/dev/sdb` and then a FILESYSTEM on top, all via the `stratis` CLI. Which sequence?
options: `stratis pool create mypool /dev/sdb` (create pool), `
`lvcreate --stratis …` — lvm doesn't manage stratis
`stratisd --create` — `stratisd` is the daemon, not the CLI
`pvcreate; stratis pool attach` — wrong CLI flow
questions.explanation: Stratis: thin-provisioned storage with snapshots. Install: dnf install stratisd stratis-cli; systemctl enable --now stratisd. Create pool: stratis pool create mypool /dev/sdb. Create filesystem: stratis filesystem create mypool myfs. Mount: mount /stratis/mypool/myfs /mnt. List: stratis pool list; stratis filesystem list.

questions.question: RHEL 8's VDO (Virtual Data Optimizer) provides INLINE deduplication + compression beneath a filesystem. The admin wants to create a VDO device on `/dev/sdb` with logical size 20 GB. Which command?
options: `mkvdo /dev/sdb --name=myvdo --size=20G` — `mkvdo` is not a real command; VDO is managed with the `vdo` utility, not `mkvdo`
`vdo create --name=myvdo --device=/dev/sdb --vdoLogicalSize=20G` — canonical syntax to create a VDO volume on `/dev/sdb` with a 20 GB logical size for inline deduplication
`vdoadm create --device=/dev/sdb --name=myvdo` — `vdoadm` is not a real command; use `vdo create` with `--device=/dev/sdb` and `--name` to create the VDO layer

`lvcreate --vdo --name=myvdo /dev/sdb` — LVM can create VDO-backed logical volumes via `lvconvert --type vdo-pool`, but the standalone VDO utility (`vdo create --device=/dev/sdb`) is the canonical RHCSA approach
questions.explanation: VDO provides deduplication and compression. Install: dnf install vdo kmod-kvdo. Create: vdo create --name=myvdo --device=/dev/sdb --vdoLogicalSize=20G. Format: mkfs.xfs -K /dev/mapper/myvdo. Mount with discard: mount -o discard /dev/mapper/myvdo /mnt. vdostats --human-readable: check savings.

questions.question: RHEL 8 replaces Docker with Podman (daemonless, rootless-capable, container-runtime). The admin wants to run an Nginx container in DETACHED mode named `myapp` mapping host port 8080 to container port 80. Which command?
options: `podman run -d --name myapp -p 8080:80 nginx` — runs the `nginx` container detached (`-d`), named `myapp` (`--name myapp`), with port 8080 mapped to container port 80 (`-p 8080:80`)
`podman start nginx --port 8080:80 --detach --name myapp` — `podman start` restarts a stopped, already-created container; it does not accept `--port`, `--name`, or create a new detached instance
`container run -d --name myapp -p 8080:80 nginx` — `container` is not a valid command on RHEL 8; the correct runtime command is `podman run` with `-d` for detached mode and `--name myapp`
`docker run -d --name myapp -p 8080:80 nginx` — Docker is not installed by default on RHEL 8+; RHEL replaced Docker with Podman; the `podman run` syntax is identical for this use case
questions.explanation: Podman: daemonless, rootless container engine. podman run -d: detached. --name: container name. -p host:container: port mapping. podman ps: list running containers. podman images: local images. podman pull registry.access.redhat.com/ubi8: pull image. podman stop/rm: stop and remove. No daemon required unlike Docker.

questions.question: RHEL ships `tuned` — a daemon that applies system-wide performance profiles (`balanced`, `desktop`, `throughput-performance`, `latency-performance`, `network-latency`, etc.). The admin wants to LIST profiles and APPLY one. Which commands?
options: `tuned-adm list` to see available profiles
`systemctl list tuned-profiles` — not a thing
`tuned list` — wrong invocation; tool is `tuned-adm`
`tune2fs --list-profiles` — tune2fs is for ext filesystems, unrelated to tuned
questions.explanation: tuned: dynamic tuning daemon. tuned-adm list: show all profiles. tuned-adm active: current profile. tuned-adm profile virtual-guest: apply profile. tuned-adm recommend: suggest profile for system type. Common profiles: balanced, throughput-performance, latency-performance, powersave, virtual-guest. systemctl enable --now tuned.

questions.question: An NFS share `nfsserver:/share` should be mounted ON DEMAND when first accessed under `/mnt/auto`, and AUTOMATICALLY UNMOUNTED after idle. The `autofs` service is for this — uses a master map + per-mount map files. Which approach?
options: `mount` + rc.local — wrong (eager mount, not on-demand)
`/etc/fstab` with auto option — fstab mounts eagerly, not on-demand
Add `/mnt/auto /etc/auto.nfs` to `/etc/auto.master`
`autofs --add` — not a real command
questions.explanation: autofs: mounts filesystems on demand. /etc/auto.master: /mnt/nfs /etc/auto.nfs --timeout=60. /etc/auto.nfs: data -rw,soft nfsserver:/export/data. systemctl enable --now autofs. Access /mnt/nfs/data to trigger mount. Unmounts after timeout. Useful for large NFS environments — only mounts what is accessed. systemctl enable autofs

questions.question: An admin needs to create a LUKS-encrypted partition on `/dev/sdb1`. The user will set a passphrase at unlock time; the data is encrypted at rest with AES-XTS. Which command initialises the LUKS header on `/dev/sdb1`?
options: `cryptsetup luksFormat /dev/sdb1`
`openssl enc -aes-256` — encrypts a file, not a block device
`cryptsetup encrypt --luks` — wrong syntax; verb is `luksFormat`
`mkluks` — not a real command
questions.explanation: LUKS encryption: cryptsetup luksFormat /dev/sdb1 (prompts for passphrase). Open: cryptsetup luksOpen /dev/sdb1 mydata → creates /dev/mapper/mydata. Format: mkfs.xfs /dev/mapper/mydata. Mount: mount /dev/mapper/mydata /mnt. Persistent: add to /etc/crypttab and /etc/fstab. cryptsetup luksDump: show header info.

questions.question: An admin bonds two physical NICs `eth0` + `eth1` into a single `bond0` interface for active-backup redundancy. Configuration must persist via NetworkManager. Which `nmcli` sequence?
options: `bonding --create` — not a real command
`nmcli con add type bond ifname bond0 mode active-backup`
`nmcli bond create` — wrong syntax
`ip link add bond0 type bond` — works at runtime but doesn't persist via NetworkManager
questions.explanation: Create bond: nmcli con add type bond ifname bond0 bond.options 'mode=active-backup'. Add slaves: nmcli con add type ethernet ifname eth0 master bond0; nmcli con add type ethernet ifname eth1 master bond0. Activate: nmcli con up bond0. cat /proc/net/bonding/bond0: check status. Modes: active-backup, balance-rr, 802.3ad (LACP). add slaves with nmcli ethernet con

questions.question: RHEL ships a web-based admin console (single binary `cockpit-ws`) exposing system info, service management, container runtime, networking, storage, software updates via a browser. Default port is 9090 over HTTPS. Which describes Cockpit and access?
options: SNMP daemon — wrong category
CLI dashboard — false; Cockpit is web-based
Graphical desktop — false; Cockpit is a web admin console, not a DE
Web admin console
questions.explanation: Cockpit: browser-based system administration. Install: dnf install cockpit. Enable: systemctl enable --now cockpit.socket. Access: https://hostname:9090. Features: services, storage, networking, logs, terminal, updates, SELinux. Firewall: firewall-cmd --add-service=cockpit --permanent. Supports multi-server management from one UI. enable with systemctl enable --now cockpit.socket then browse port 9090

questions.question: RHEL 8 introduces APPLICATION STREAMS (AppStreams) — multiple parallel versions of a package shipped as `modules`. The admin wants to list streams of `nodejs` then enable the 18 stream before installation. Which sequence?
options: `dnf appstream list / install` — not the actual subcommand names
`dnf stream list nodejs` — not a real subcommand
`dnf module list` (lists all module streams), `dnf module enable nodejs:18`
`subscription-manager repos --enable nodejs-18` — that's different (manages repos, not modules)
questions.explanation: DNF modules (RHEL 8 AppStream): dnf module list: see all modules and streams. dnf module list nodejs: check available streams. dnf module enable nodejs:18: switch to version 18 stream. dnf module install nodejs:18/common: install default profile. dnf module reset nodejs: reset to default. Allows multiple versions of software coexisting. dnf install nodejs

questions.question: A daily backup job syncs `/var/data/` from a local RHEL host to `backup@remote:/backups/data/`. The transfer must be INCREMENTAL (only changed files), preserve permissions / timestamps / ownership, USE SSH for transport, and COMPRESS over the wire. Which command?
options: `rsync --copy` — not a real flag
`rsync -avz /var/data/ backup@remote:/backups/data/`
`ftp put` — FTP isn't suitable (no SSH; deprecated)
`scp -r` — copies but not incremental; transfers everything every run
questions.explanation: rsync -avz: -a archive mode (preserves permissions, timestamps, symlinks), -v verbose, -z compress during transfer. Trailing slash on source copies contents only (not parent dir). --delete: remove files at destination not in source. --dry-run: preview without changes. rsync over SSH by default. --exclude='*.log': skip patterns. Efficient: only transfers changed blocks.

questions.question: You added a new disk and created an XFS filesystem on /dev/sdb1. Which TWO steps are required to mount it persistently at /data after reboot?
options: Add an entry for /dev/sdb1 (or its UUID) to /etc/fstab
Run `systemctl daemon-reload` so systemd picks up the new fstab entry
Reboot the system to confirm the mount unit fires correctly
Run `mkdir /data` if the mount point doesn't exist
questions.explanation: fstab plus an existing mount point are the two prerequisites. `daemon-reload` is needed if you write a *.mount unit by hand, not for fstab edits (systemd-fstab-generator picks them up on boot or `systemctl daemon-reload`). Rebooting is a verification step, not a requirement — `mount -a` confirms it works without a reboot.
